source_text: Ne illa quidem impatientiae species excusatur, [in amissione nostrorum] cui aliqua doloris patrocinatur adsertio. praeponendus est enim respectus denuntiationis apostoli, qui ait: ne contristemini dormitione cuiusquam, sicut nationes, quae spe carent. et merito. credentes enim resurrectionem Christi in nostram quoque credimus. propter quos ille et obiit et resurrexit. ergo cum constet de resurrectione mortuorum, uacat dolor mortis, uacat et impa* tientia doloris. cur enim doleas, si perisse non credis? cur impatienter feras subductum interim quem credis reuersurum? profectio est quam putas mortem. non est lugendus qui antecedit, sed plane desiderandus. id quoque desiderium patientia temperandum. cur enim. immoderate feras. abisse quem mox, subsequeris? ceterum impatientia in huiusmodi et spei nostrae male ominatur et fidem praeuaricatur. et Christum laedimus, cum euocatos quosque ab illo quasi miserandos non aequanimiter accipimus. cupio, inquit apostolus, recipi iam et esse cum domino. quanto melius ostendit uotum! Christianorum ergo uotum, si alios consecutos impatienter dolemus, ipsi consequi nolumus.
thought_title: Grief at the death of believers is impatience
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that even the grief felt at the loss of loved ones is a form of impatience, because Christians believe in the resurrection.
pass_a_gloss: Not even that kind of impatience is excused, in the loss of our own people, for which some assertion of grief pleads as advocate. For the regard for the apostle's warning must be placed first, who says: do not be saddened by the sleep of anyone, like the pagans, who lack hope. And rightly so. For believing in the resurrection of Christ, we believe also in our own. For their sake he both died and rose again. Therefore, since it is established concerning the resurrection of the dead, grief over death is empty, and impatience of grief is also empty. For why would you grieve, if you do not believe that he has perished? Why would you bear impatiently the one who has been taken away for a time, whom you believe is going to return? It is a departure that you think is death. The one who goes ahead is not to be mourned, but plainly to be longed for. This longing also must be tempered by patience. For why would you bear immoderately that the one whom you will soon follow has gone away? Moreover, impatience in matters of this kind both speaks ill of our hope and transgresses faith. And we injure Christ, when we do not receive with equanimity all those who have been called away by him, as if they were to be pitied. I desire, says the apostle, to be received already and to be with the Lord. How much better he shows the wish! Therefore the wish of Christians: if we grieve impatiently that others have attained it, we ourselves do not wish to attain it.

pass_b_english: Not even that form of impatience is excused—the one in the loss of our own people—for which some claim of grief pleads as advocate. The apostle's warning must be placed first. He says: Do not be saddened by anyone's sleep, as the pagans are, who lack hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And rightly so. For since we believe in Christ's resurrection, we believe in our own as well, because it was for us that he both died and rose again. Therefore, since the resurrection of the dead is certain, grief over death is empty, and impatience in grief is empty too. Why should you grieve if you do not believe the person has perished? Why should you bear impatiently the temporary removal of someone you believe will return? It is a departure that you think is death. The one who goes ahead is not to be mourned, but certainly to be longed for. And that longing too must be tempered by patience. Why should you bear immoderately the departure of someone you will soon follow? Besides, impatience in such matters speaks ill of our hope and violates our faith. We also wrong Christ when we do not accept with equanimity those he has called away, as if they were to be pitied. I long, the apostle says, to be received now and to be with the Lord (Philippians 1:23). How much better he shows his desire! So if we grieve impatiently when others have attained the desire of Christians, we ourselves do not want to attain it.
notes: The source text has 'impa* tientia' with an asterisk and space, indicating a line break or minor damage in the manuscript; the word is clearly impatientia.

problems.quote: I long, the apostle says, to be received now and to be with the Lord (Philippians 1:23)
problems.why: Paul says 'to depart and be with Christ,' not 'to be received now.'
problems.fix: Correct to 'to depart and be with Christ.'

fixed: The English 'to be received now' misstates the source 'recipi iam' in context: the apostle's wish is to depart (be released from this life) and be with Christ, not to be received. Corrected to 'to depart and be with Christ'.
